html:
I’ve been Chinese for over thirty years, and a Houston Rockets fan for nearly half of them. I really wish this hadn’t happened.

My overriding feeling is helplessness.

I won’t say who’s right or wrong, I won’t talk politics, and I won’t denounce anyone for whitewashing or cheerleading for anyone. These are just some thoughts of mine.

Differences in culture and values mean we can’t possibly agree on a lot of things. When I brought this up with a European colleague, before I could even get out the arguments I’d carefully prepared, he shut me up with one line: “So the whole NBA gets killed off because of one person’s one sentence?” Yes, the principle being invoked here is “freedom of speech.” Preconceptions are very hard to change. Maybe that’s also why first impressions matter so much when you meet a stranger. Once “freedom of speech is being restricted” has set the terms, it makes no difference if I then go through, point by point, the stories behind it all: Chinese sovereignty, the situation in Hong Kong and so on. Look at it from the other side, and it’s the same reason we got angry the moment we heard the news. “Whoever offends China shall be punished, however far away,” as the old Han-dynasty battle cry goes: that’s our preconception, or rather our bottom line, so any insincere apology afterward is useless too, and may only make things worse. Morey, the Rockets’ general manager, was probably lying on the sofa at home, scrolling, saw the pictures from Hong Kong and casually shared one, just as they bash Trump every day. He may be a general manager and a shrewd calculator, but on this he slipped up. Or rather, he represents a certain type of so-called “Westerner”: mention China and it’s a dictatorship, OK, which runs against the “freedom of speech” in their blood, so sharing that Hong Kong post, like passing on a lucky koi meme, fit their values. Right, off it goes. His reaction afterward bears this out: he never expected it to cause such an uproar in China. He clearly didn’t understand what was really going on, which also suggests that his so-called support for Hong Kong came from the same place: he hadn’t done his homework.

Back to where the last paragraph started: differences in culture and values. As it happens, the last time I spent half the night explaining China to a German colleague was in 2017, in Hong Kong. I don’t know the US well enough to comment, but in the eyes of ordinary Europeans, most Chinese people fall into the category of “mysterious Eastern forces.” My German colleague said he had almost no interaction with the Chinese students at his institute. His impression was that they came to Germany, attended classes and wrote their theses at the institute, got their degrees and left. After several years, he knew nothing at all about them. And with roughly half the people in the library being Chinese students, he was very puzzled. In fact, his view is typical of how most Europeans (in my experience, the Dutch and the Germans) see Chinese people. In 1840, China’s doors were forced open, and I’m sure everyone knows what happened over the hundred-plus years until 1949: turmoil and insecurity, our fate always dictated by “Westerners.” What national identity, what confidence, could there be? After the Industrial Revolution, Western society and its institutions swept the world. We missed that wave of development and were bullied on top of it, and by 1949 we had fallen behind by who knows how many years. We’ve largely closed the economic gap in a few decades, but the rest isn’t so simple: education, the rule of law, national self-confidence and more. So, 1949 came, the era of bowing and scraping to white Westerners ended, and a new round of “learning the barbarians’ superior skills to make ourselves strong” began. Hang on: these “barbarians” are the very Western societies that used to bully us. So after being beaten up, we had to learn from our attackers; that’s how we’ve spent the past few decades. This whole chain of events over 150-plus years has left us with very complicated feelings toward white Westerners. Add a thousand years of Confucian upbringing, and the Chinese person standing in front of a Westerner is the outward expression of all these complicated things. From attacker, to teacher, to competitor; from our old fear of foreigners to slowly learning to walk on our own and going abroad, only to find we still had to learn their languages to talk to them and learn their technology. All along the way, we’ve trodden very carefully. Obviously, Westerners don’t see any of this. I once even chatted with an Italian friend who had no idea Italy was part of the Eight-Nation Alliance that invaded China in 1900. What they see are some short, yellow-skinned, inarticulate, shy, mysterious Easterners. Fortunately, all this is slowly changing, especially when I see the knowledge and English of kids born after 2000 and 2010, and above all their self-confidence and ideas, which are orders of magnitude beyond what we children of the 1980s had growing up. We are slowly realizing that the country has grown stronger and our voice in the world keeps rising, but we also face a lot of pressure. As the saying goes, the tallest tree in the forest is the first to be broken by the wind, and voices of opposition and doubt come one after another.

And at this moment, the differences in culture and values collided head-on.

In my years in Europe, the Europeans I’ve seen are roughly this combination: a sense of democratic superiority + the arrogance and superiority that come from two hundred years of crushing China and the Chinese in every respect + the unavoidable pride of being the cultural and economic mainstream + contempt rooted in the stereotype of Chinese people as silent, opinionless and easily controlled. Although the vast majority of people are very nice. Racial discrimination is very rare, but the inner world strung together by these plus signs shows through from time to time. Take the frequent double standards, or this NBA business, where my colleague shut me down with one sentence. Every time something like this happens, it sticks in my craw. My colleagues often joke, for example, that Chinese companies love to copy. Sadly, it’s true, though our own R&D is getting stronger. I gave them the examples of Made in Germany in the early 20th century and of postwar Japan, and told them that copying is a necessary stage on the road to doing your own R&D, but it didn’t help much: preconceptions still ruled. Putting myself in their shoes, I felt deeply helpless. There’s no one to blame, because this is something close to genetic; call it values for now, or stereotypes. To use an imperfect analogy: walking down an empty street in the middle of the night, we probably feel differently depending on whether a white person or a Black person is coming toward us. Stereotypes are hard to change, but they aren’t set in stone; it just takes time. We have gradually started to speak up, and Westerners aren’t quite used to it. But when we speak up, to borrow the NBA’s official language, regrettably, we can’t rule out that many people are using personal attacks to get what they want, such as cursing Morey’s whole family or making remarks about 9/11. By the usual Western line, that’s freedom of speech, OK. But if we want to earn respect and a voice, seeing who can shout loudest and march in the neatest formation backfires. What we need is logic and rational, fact-based argument, so that more Westerners come to understand us, our thinking and our country. That’s the precondition for earning respect and raising our international standing. I also hope the West will learn more about China, stop assuming that whatever differs from them doesn’t exist or makes no sense, and look at the world afresh, with an eye to how it is changing.
